result.markdown: --- title: "optiDoseR in nlmixr2" description: "A full nlmixr2 workflow with optiDoseR: fit the warfarin PKPD model and estimate the optimal dose for the typical patient." aliases: - /optiDoseR_nlmixr_warf.html # The code needs nlmixr2, optiDoseR, and a fitted model that is not part of # this repository, so it is shown but not run; figures are pre-rendered. execute: eval: false --- Using optiDoseR with nlmixr2 allows to have a full pharmacometrics (PMX) workflow of preparing data, fitting and estimating PMX parameters, and estimating optimal typical and individual doses to fulfill a therapeutic goal. ## Loading libraries For the entire workflow, the tidyverse package is utilized for data processing, the nlmixr2 package for fitting the data and simulating, and the optiDoseR package to generate the required model code for estimating doses. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(optiDoseR) library(tidyverse) library(nlmixr2) ``` ::: ## Warfarin PKPD model In this example, we're looking at the prominent warfarin PKPD example. To this end, the structural model for a one-compartment PKPD model with indirect response is set up in the nlmixr2 model-structure as described here. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple"} ## See model code ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pk.turnover <- function() { ini({ tktr <- log(1) tka <- log(1) tcl <- log(0.1) tv <- log(10) ## eta.ktr ~ 1 eta.ka ~ 1 eta.cl ~ 2 eta.v ~ 1 prop.err <- 0.1 pkadd.err <- 0.1 ## temax <- logit(0.8) tec50 <- log(0.5) tkout <- log(0.05) te0 <- log(100) ## eta.emax ~ .5 eta.ec50 ~ .5 eta.kout ~ .5 eta.e0 ~ .5 ## pdadd.err <- 10 }) model({ ktr <- exp(tktr + eta.ktr) ka <- exp(tka + eta.ka) cl <- exp(tcl + eta.cl) v <- exp(tv + eta.v) emax = expit(temax+eta.emax) ec50 = exp(tec50 + eta.ec50) kout = exp(tkout + eta.kout) e0 = exp(te0 + eta.e0) ## DCP = center/v PD=1-emax*DCP/(ec50+DCP) ## effect(0) = e0 kin = e0*kout ## d/dt(depot) = -ktr * depot d/dt(gut) = ktr * depot -ka * gut d/dt(center) = ka * gut - cl / v * center d/dt(effect) = kin*PD -kout*effect ## cp = center / v cp ~ prop(prop.err) + add(pkadd.err) effect ~ add(pdadd.err) | pca }) } ``` ::: ::: ## Fitting the data Next, we can fit the model to the warfarin data with the nlmixr function to estimate the typical and individual PKPD parameters. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fit <- nlmixr(pk.turnover, warfarin, "saem") ``` ::: ## Setting up the OptiProject Based on the fitted nlmixr2 model, we can set up a OptiProject. The OptiProject gathers all information required to generate the model code and data for the optiDose approach. The OptiProject is set up with the `newOptiProject` function, where you have to define the software for the OptiProject, in this case "nlmixr2". Then you can load the structural model and estimated typical and individual parameters from your fitted nlmixr2 object through `addPmxRun`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} warfProj <- newOptiProject("nlmixr2") %>% addPmxRun(fit) ``` ::: Second, therapeutic targets can be added. In this case, we want the effect compartment not to fall below 30 over the time-period from 0 to 200 with the `addConstraintAUC` function, while the drug exposure is as large as possible, done with the `addSecondaryAUC` function. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} warfProj <- warfProj %>% addConstraintAUC(state = "effect", limit = 30, pen_time = c(0,200), eval_time = 200, pen_values="below") %>% addSecondaryAUC(state = "cp", pen_values = "low", pen_time = c(0,200), eval_time = 200) ``` ::: Finally, we need to define, what dose levels we want to estimate. Here, we just want to estimate one dose at time-point 0, and we set the initial estimate to 100. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} warfProj <- warfProj %>% addDoseLevel(time=0,ini_est=100) ``` ::: ## Estimating typical doses With all the required information gathered in the OptiProject object `warfProj`, we can call the `saveOptiProject` function to transform the information into model code and data. We can give it a name, so the new model is saved as *name*_model and the data as *name*_data. Here, we only want to utilize the typical parameter estimates, so we set *pop = FALSE*. Since we are working with nlmixr2, we can directly run the created model with *run_nlmixr2 = TRUE*. The fitted object will be called *name*_fit. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} saveOptiProject(warfProj, name = "warfOptiModel_typical", pop = FALSE, run_nlmixr2 = TRUE) ``` ::: ## Simulation for typical patient To check, whether the estimated dose really fulfills the defined therapeutic target, we can use the fitted model from the OptiProject to perform simulations. We create an eventTable with equal sampling time-points between 0 and 200. We also need the data with the previously estimated typical PKPD parameters. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ev_typical <- eventTable() %>% add.dosing(dose = 1) %>% add.sampling(0:200) %>% et(id=1) cov_data_typical <- warfOptiModel_typical_data %>% filter(TIME==0) %>% select(-c(TIME,DV,AMT,EVID,MDV)) sim_typical <- rxSolve(warfOptiModel_typical_fit, events = ev_typical, iCov=cov_data_typical) sim_typical_data <- as.data.frame(sim_typical) %>% pivot_longer(cols=c("cp","effect"), names_to = "Compartment", values_to = "DV") ``` ::: ## Results As can be seen in the plot, the effect-compartment perfectly matches the predefined therapeutic target of 30, meaning that the estimated dose of 41.6 mg leads to maximal drug exposure that does not violate the constraint. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Plot code"} ggplot(sim_typical_data,aes(x=time,y=DV)) + geom_hline(data = sim_typical_data %>% filter(Compartment == "effect"), aes(yintercept = 30), col = "red", linewidth=2) + geom_line(linewidth=2) + facet_wrap(~Compartment, scales = "free") ``` ::: ![](images/nlmixr2-typical-simulation.png){fig-alt="Simulated concentration and effect for the typical patient; the effect reaches but does not fall below the target of 30."} ## Continuance In the tutorial [optiDoseR in nlmixr2 with IIV](nlmixr2-warfarin-iiv.qmd), the here presented concept is extended to estimate doses not only for the typical patient, but for all individuals in the original warfarin PKPD dataset.
